title: When Seeing Is No Longer Believing: What Happens When Our Trust Signals Stop Working?
summary: Trust signals like faces, voices, and personal details are easier to fake. Discover how to respond and strengthen fraud prevention.
body_markdown:
For years, one of the simplest pieces of anti-fraud advice has been to verify what you’re being told. If an email feels suspicious, call the person. If you’re not sure who’s messaging you, speak to them directly. If there’s still doubt, get them on video.


As the technology powering scams becomes more sophisticated, that logic is beginning to break down. In January 2024, an employee at a multinational company in Hong Kong received a phishing message from someone impersonating the Chief Financial Officer of the company’s UK head office.


The employee was invited to a video conference about confidential transactions, where the CFO appeared to be present. They subsequently authorized transfers totaling around HK$200 million. Hong Kong Police later concluded that[publicly available video and audio had been used](https://www.info.gov.hk/gia/general/202406/26/P2024062600192.htm) to create a fake, pre-recorded conference.


What makes the case so unsettling isn’t simply the sophistication of the technology. It’s that the scam exploits exactly the thing we would normally use to establish trust. Eyeballing another person is supposed to provide reassurance (and has worked for millennia). Hearing someone’s voice was supposed to make the request more credible, too. In this case, both signals became part of the deception.


The U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC)[reported that U.S. consumers lost $3.5 billion to impersonation scams in 2025](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/06/ftc-data-show-people-reported-losing-3-point-5-billion-imposter-scams-2025) , and impersonation represented nearly one in three fraud reports.


All of this raises a much bigger question than whether deepfakes are getting harder to spot. If a familiar face, a recognized voice, or a convincing video call can no longer be treated as reliable proof, what should take their place?


## We’ve Been Borrowing Trust from the Physical World


Most digital interactions still rely on cues borrowed from the physical world. We recognize a face on a video call or receive a message that includes information only a trusted person or organization should know. None of these signals has ever been foolproof, but they help us make quick judgments about whether an interaction feels genuine.


We rely on familiar signals because, historically, they have been difficult enough to reproduce convincingly that they provided useful reassurance. Customers shouldn’t feel the need to perform a forensic investigation every time they receive a call from their bank or join a Teams meeting with a colleague.


AI is weakening that assumption. Voices can be cloned. Images and video can be synthesized. Personal details scraped from social media, data breaches, and public sources can make the whole interaction feel even more convincing.


The very things we once used as evidence of authenticity are becoming easier to manufacture.[In a recent UK survey](https://www.ofcom.org.uk/online-safety/illegal-and-harmful-content/deepfakes-demean-defraud-disinform?) , 43% of adults said they’d encountered a deepfake in the previous six months, but only 9% felt confident identifying one.


## The Economics of Deception Have Been Transformed


The erosion of those trust signals matters even more because AI has dramatically reduced the cost of deception. Creating a convincing scam used to require considerable effort. Criminals needed people to research targets, write and translate messages, make calls, create false identities, and keep conversations going. The more personalized the scam, the more time and people it generally required. Generative AI removes many of those constraints.


Scammers can now reach far more people while making each approach feel far less generic. The badly written phishing email addressed to “Dear Customer” hasn’t disappeared, but it now sits alongside something much more persuasive: a message in natural language, closely tailored to an individual, and supported by synthetic audio and video. INTERPOL’s[own 2026 global assessment](https://www.interpol.int/News-and-Events/News/2026/INTERPOL-report-warns-of-increasingly-sophisticated-global-financial-fraud-threat) estimates that AI-enhanced fraud is 4.5 times more profitable than traditional methods.


Trust signals are weakening just as the machinery used to exploit them is becoming cheaper and faster. A scammer no longer needs to know you in any meaningful sense to sound as though they do. A message can reference somewhere you have traveled, an event you attended, or an interest you have discussed publicly. Even something as personal as a bereavement could be used to manufacture an emotional connection with someone and make the approach feel credible.


This matters because “something only they would know” has traditionally carried a lot of weight. Increasingly, it may prove only that the information existed somewhere online. The challenge for organizations is therefore much broader than detecting synthetic faces or cloned voices. They also need to recognize that personal knowledge itself can now be manufactured into a convincing trust signal.


## Trust the Process, Not Just the Person


If faces, voices, and personal knowledge are becoming easier to imitate, organizations need to move more of the burden of trust into the process surrounding an interaction.


The first shift is toward **independent verification** . If someone calls claiming to be from your bank, the safest verification is never inside the same conversation. Instead, end the call and contact the bank through a number or app you already trust. The same principle applies inside a business.


An unexpected request from a senior executive to move money should be confirmed through a separate, established channel, rather than through contact details supplied with the request itself. This is not particularly futuristic technology. In fact, the FBI has long recommended verifying payment changes and transactions in person or via a known telephone number.


In this way, the question shifts from “Is this person who they claim to be?” to “Can this request be independently verified?” The first question asks us to judge the authenticity of what’s in front of us. The second asks whether the request can survive contact with something the scammer does not control.


The next layer is **context and behavior** . A voice may sound exactly like the customer. Their identity document may look genuine. But does the surrounding activity around make sense? Is this a device they normally use? Are they suddenly making a transaction unlike any they’ve made before?


None of those signals prove fraud in isolation, but together they can provide a much richer picture. Detection will increasingly need to rely on behavioral analysis rather than document verification alone.


That also means favoring **process over appearance** . The Hong Kong deepfake case is a useful warning precisely *because* everybody on the video call could appear convincing… and yet the request was still false.


Organizations therefore need controls that can withstand even a “perfect” impersonation. High-risk payments might require dual authorization, confirmation through a separate system, or additional checks triggered by unusual behavior. There is unlikely to be one magic “deepfake detector.” The point is to make sure that the riskiest actions cannot be authorized purely because someone looks, sounds, or behaves convincingly.


A similar shift is occurring in **identity provenance** . The[latest digital identity guidance](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63a.html) from the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) recommends a combination of measures for remote identity proofing, including protected channels, analyzing media for signs of manipulation, confirming that content is coming from a genuine capture device, liveness techniques, and human review. It also warns that biometric comparison alone cannot defeat every forged-media attack.


We are moving away from a world in which one convincing signal can settle the question and toward one in which trust requires several independent pieces of evidence. Identity, behavior, device, channel, provenance, and the nature of the request can all contribute. If one signal turns out to have been faked, the others are still there.


## The Foundations of Trust Are Changing


It is tempting to assume that the end point is a world in which nobody believes anything. If faces can be faked, voices can be cloned, and personal details can be gathered and repackaged at scale, then isn’t every interaction suspect to some degree?


That is not especially useful, and it is not where this needs to lead. The goal has to be to build processes robust enough that customers do not have to be suspicious of everything they see and hear.


For years, digital interactions have borrowed reassurance from signals that were once difficult to reproduce convincingly: a familiar face, a recognized voice, a document, or a piece of personal knowledge. Those signals can no longer be relied upon in isolation.


A stronger model builds trust from several signals at once: independent verification, behavioral context, secure processes, and technical controls, all supported by human judgment. In that environment, a synthetic voice or convincing video becomes far less powerful, because the scam still has to survive the rest of the process around it.


In an age of deepfakes, authenticity will increasingly need to be shown rather than simply assumed.[The organizations that understand this will be best placed to preserve the thing scams are really trying to exploit in the first place: our trust.](https://www.concentrix.com/services-solutions/financial-crimes-compliance/)
